(ch10-sec-opener)=
## A Kern County opener: did almond yield really change?

Kern County is one of the most productive farm counties in the United States,
and almonds are one of its signature crops. Suppose a grower looks back at the
last nine crop years and asks a simple question: **"Is our typical almond yield
really about one ton per acre, or is it drifting?"**

We can put a number on the "typical" yield. Using the curated teaching dataset
`kern_crops_sim`, the mean almond **yield per acre** across the nine crop years
2015–2023 is **1.0359 tons per acre** (dataset-derived from `kern_crops_sim`,
variable `yield_per_acre`; see the codebook `data/codebooks/kern_crops_sim.md`).

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-opener-stat
crops  <- read.csv("data/processed/kern_crops_sim.csv")
almond <- subset(crops, commodity == "ALMONDS")
mean(~yield_per_acre, data = almond)   # dataset-derived: 1.0359 tons/acre
```

:::{important} This is simulated data — read this before you cite a number
`kern_crops_sim` is a **synthetic** dataset (note the `_sim` suffix). It was
generated by a seeded script because the real USDA NASS Quick Stats feed
requires an email-registered API key the autonomous build could not provision.
The magnitudes are *plausible for Kern County* but they are **not measured
values**, and no number here is a factual claim about real almond farming. We
use it because it is perfect for *learning the method*. Every technique you see
works identically on the real data once a key is registered. (See
`data/codebooks/kern_crops_sim.md`.)
:::

That sample mean of 1.0359 is *close* to one ton per acre — but it is built from
only nine years, and yields wobble from year to year with the weather. So the
honest question is not "is 1.0359 exactly 1?" (it never will be), but: **is the
gap between 1.0359 and 1 large enough to be real, or is it the kind of wobble we
would expect from nine noisy years even if the true long-run mean were exactly
1?** That is a question about a **population mean**, and this chapter is the tool
for it: the **t-test family**.

(ch10-sec-objectives)=
## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. **(Apply)** Conduct a one-sample $t$-test and confidence interval for a mean,
   and state the conditions the $t$-distribution requires.
2. **(Apply)** Conduct a paired $t$-test by analyzing the differences, and
   explain when pairing is the right design.
3. **(Apply)** Conduct a two-sample $t$-test and confidence interval for a
   difference of means.
4. **(Analyze)** Choose between a paired and a two-sample procedure for a given
   study design, and justify the choice.
5. **(Evaluate)** Assess the normality and independence conditions and judge how
   robust the $t$ procedures are when those conditions bend.

**Durable skills this chapter builds:** quantitative reasoning (QR) and critical
thinking (CT).

**Before this chapter** you should be comfortable with confidence intervals
(Chapter 7) and the logic of hypothesis testing — null/alternative hypotheses,
p-values, and significance level (Chapter 8).

(ch10-sec-whyt)=
## Why a *t* and not a *z*? The intuition

### Intuition

In Chapter 6 you learned that a sample mean $\bar{x}$ varies from sample to
sample, and the size of that variation — the **standard error** — is the
population standard deviation divided by $\sqrt{n}$. To turn $\bar{x}$ into a
test we standardize it: we measure how many standard errors $\bar{x}$ sits away
from the value we are testing.

There is one practical snag. The standard error needs the *population* standard
deviation $\sigma$, and we almost never know it. We have to estimate it with the
*sample* standard deviation $s$. That substitution adds a second source of
uncertainty: not only is $\bar{x}$ noisy, but our ruler for measuring its noise
is *itself* estimated from the same small sample.

The fix is to use a distribution that is a little more spread out than the normal
— heavier in the tails — to honestly reflect that extra uncertainty. That
distribution is **Student's $t$**. With few observations the $t$ is noticeably
wider than the normal; as the sample grows, the estimate of $s$ settles down and
the $t$ becomes indistinguishable from the normal. The amount of extra spread is
controlled by one number, the **degrees of freedom**.

### Formula

The **one-sample $t$ statistic** is

```{math}
:label: ch10-eq-tstat

t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}},
```

where

- $\bar{x}$ = the **sample mean** (the average of your data),
- $\mu_0$ (read "mu-naught") = the **hypothesized population mean** — the value
  in the null hypothesis,
- $s$ = the **sample standard deviation** (your estimate of the spread),
- $n$ = the **sample size** (number of observations),
- $s/\sqrt{n}$ = the **standard error of the mean**, written $\mathrm{SE}$,
- and we compare $t$ to a **$t$-distribution with $df = n - 1$ degrees of
  freedom**. ($df$, "degrees of freedom," is the single number that sets how
  heavy the tails are; here it is one less than the sample size.)

The two-sided p-value is the probability, *if $H_0$ were true*, of a $t$ at least
as far from zero as the one we observed.

The **confidence interval** for $\mu$ inverts the same machinery:

```{math}
:label: ch10-eq-tci

\bar{x} \;\pm\; t^{\star}_{df}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}},
```

where $t^{\star}_{df}$ (read "t-star") is the **critical value**: the point on
the $t$-distribution with $df$ degrees of freedom that puts the chosen
confidence level (say 95%) in the middle.

### R

In R, the one-sample procedure is `t.test()`. With `mosaic` you can write it in the
formula form `t.test(~variable, data = , mu = )`, where `mu` is the value $\mu_0$
you are testing against. Its output is compact — the statistic, degrees of freedom,
p-value, confidence interval, and sample mean — which we unpack line by line in
Worked Example 1:

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-whyt-demo
:tags: [remove-output]
# (Run for real in @ch10-sec-ex1 below; shown here only to introduce the function.)
t.test(~yield_per_acre, data = almond, mu = 1.0)
```

:::{note} One function, three jobs
You only need **one** function for this entire chapter — base R's `t.test()` — in
three shapes:

- `t.test(~y, data = D, mu = )` — the **one-sample** test and CI.
- `t.test(~diff, data = D)` — the **paired** test, run on a column of within-pair
  **differences** (a paired test is just a one-sample test on the differences).
- `t.test(y ~ g, data = D)` — the **two-sample** test, with the response `y` split
  by a two-level group `g`.
:::

(ch10-sec-onesample)=
## The one-sample t-test

### Intuition

Use a one-sample $t$-test when you have **one group** of measurements and a
**specific number** you want to compare its mean against — a standard, a target,
a historical value, a claim. "Is the mean wait time under 15 minutes?" "Is the
average fill weight 12 ounces?" "Is the typical almond yield one ton per acre?"

### Formula

Exactly @ch10-eq-tstat and @ch10-eq-tci above. The hypotheses are

$$
H_0:\ \mu = \mu_0 \qquad\text{vs.}\qquad H_A:\ \mu \ne \mu_0
$$

(or $<$ / $>$ for a one-sided test). **Conditions** for the $t$ procedure:

1. **Independence** — observations are independent (a random sample, or fewer
   than 10% of a finite population).
2. **Normality / sample size** — the data come from a roughly normal population,
   *or* the sample is large enough ($n \ge 30$ is the usual rule of thumb) for
   the Central Limit Theorem to make $\bar{x}$ approximately normal. For small
   $n$, check that the data are roughly symmetric with no extreme outliers.

(ch10-sec-ex1)=
### Worked Example 1 — almond yield vs. one ton per acre (Kern data)

**Intuition.** Back to the opener. We have nine yearly almond yields and one
benchmark, $\mu_0 = 1$ ton per acre. One group, one number to compare against:
a one-sample $t$-test.

**Formula.** $H_0:\ \mu = 1$ vs. $H_A:\ \mu \ne 1$, using @ch10-eq-tstat with
$df = 9 - 1 = 8$.

**Computation.**

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-ex1-onesample
t.test(~yield_per_acre, data = almond, mu = 1.0)
```

The pieces, recomputed and dataset-derived from `kern_crops_sim`:
$\bar{x} = 1.0359$ tons/acre (R's `mean of x`), $s = 0.0765$, $n = 9$, so
$\mathrm{SE} = 0.0765/\sqrt{9} = 0.0255$ and

$$
t = \frac{1.0359 - 1}{0.0255} = 1.408, \qquad df = 8.
$$

R prints exactly this: **`t = 1.4082, df = 8`**, a two-sided **`p-value = 0.1967`**,
and a `95 percent confidence interval` of **`0.977` to `1.095`** tons per acre.

**Interpretation.** Because $p = 0.197 \ge 0.05$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$.
There is not enough evidence to say the long-run mean almond yield differs from
one ton per acre. The confidence interval tells the same story a richer way: one
ton per acre sits comfortably *inside* (0.977, 1.095), so it remains a plausible
value for the true mean. The 0.0359 gap we saw in the opener is exactly the kind
of wobble nine noisy years can produce on their own.

:::{tip} The decision and the interval always agree
For a two-sided test at level $\alpha$, you reject $H_0:\ \mu = \mu_0$ **exactly
when** $\mu_0$ falls *outside* the $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval. Here $\mu_0
= 1$ is inside (0.977, 1.095), and indeed we failed to reject. The p-value and
the interval are two views of the same computation — if they ever disagree, you
have made an arithmetic error.
:::

### A picture of the data

A small sample earns a look before a test. Are the nine yields roughly symmetric
with no wild outlier? @ch10-fig-almond-hist shows they are.

```r
xbar <- mean(~yield_per_acre, data = almond)
gf_histogram(~yield_per_acre, data = almond, bins = 6,
             fill = okabe_ito[1], color = "white") %>%
  gf_vline(xintercept = ~xbar, color = okabe_ito[4],
           linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) %>%
  gf_labs(
    x = "Almond yield (tons per acre), 2015–2023 — SIMULATED",
    y = "Number of crop years",
    title = "Almond yield per acre is roughly symmetric (kern_crops_sim)",
    subtitle = paste0("Dashed line = mean = ", signif(xbar, 4))
  )
```

(ch10-fig-almond-hist)=

![A histogram of nine almond yield-per-acre values from the kern_crops_sim dataset, spanning roughly 0.92 to 1.16 tons per acre. The bars form a single rough mound with no isolated extreme value, and a vertical reference line marks the sample mean near 1.04 tons per acre.](data:image/png;base64,)

*Nine almond yields cluster between about 0.9 and 1.2 tons per acre with no extreme outlier, so the t-procedure's normality condition is reasonable for this small sample.*

(ch10-sec-paired)=
## The paired t-test

### Intuition

Sometimes two columns of numbers are **naturally matched, one-to-one**: a
before-and-after measurement on the *same* person, the left and right hand of the
*same* athlete, a 2015 and a 2023 value for the *same* crop. When the data come in
matched pairs, the smart move is to **subtract within each pair** and analyze the
single column of differences. Pairing strips away the variation *between*
subjects (some crops are just bigger than others) so the variation *within* a
pair (did this crop grow or shrink?) stands out on its own.

A paired $t$-test is therefore **not a new test at all** — it is a one-sample
$t$-test run on the differences, testing whether their mean is zero.

### Formula

Let $d_i = (\text{value 1})_i - (\text{value 2})_i$ be the **difference** for
pair $i$. Then with

- $\bar{d}$ = the **mean of the differences**,
- $s_d$ = the **standard deviation of the differences**,
- $n$ = the **number of pairs**,

the statistic is

```{math}
:label: ch10-eq-paired

t = \frac{\bar{d} - \mu_0}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}, \qquad df = n - 1,
```

where $\mu_0$ is the hypothesized mean difference (almost always $0$: "no
change"). Everything else — p-value, confidence interval — is the one-sample
machinery applied to the $d_i$.

(ch10-sec-ex2)=
### Worked Example 2 — did Kern crop acreage shift from 2015 to 2023? (Kern data)

**Intuition.** For each of eight Kern commodities we have its **harvested acres**
in 2015 and again in 2023. The two columns are matched **by commodity** — almonds
to almonds, cotton to cotton — and they share the same unit (acres). That is a
paired design. We ask: across these crops, did acreage change on average?

**Formula.** $d_i = (\text{acres}_{2023})_i - (\text{acres}_{2015})_i$ for each
commodity; $H_0:\ \mu_d = 0$ vs. $H_A:\ \mu_d \ne 0$, via @ch10-eq-paired with
$df = 8 - 1 = 7$.

**Computation.** First reshape the data so each commodity is one row with a 2015
column and a 2023 column (that plumbing is hidden below; the resulting paired table
is shown):

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-ex2-reshape
:tags: [remove-input]
# (Reshaping plumbing hidden — it aligns each commodity's 2015 and 2023 acreage
# into one row. The resulting paired table, one row per crop, is what matters:)
yr2015 <- crops[crops$year == 2015, c("commodity", "harvested_acres")]
yr2023 <- crops[crops$year == 2023, c("commodity", "harvested_acres")]
names(yr2015)[2] <- "acres_2015"
names(yr2023)[2] <- "acres_2023"
paired_crops <- merge(yr2015, yr2023, by = "commodity")
paired_crops
```

Now the paired test. Subtract *within* each pair to get one column of differences,
then run a one-sample $t$-test on that column — that **is** the paired test:

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-ex2-paired
paired_crops$diff <- paired_crops$acres_2023 - paired_crops$acres_2015
t.test(~diff, data = paired_crops, mu = 0)
```

Dataset-derived from `kern_crops_sim`: the differences have mean
$\bar{d} = 8193.25$ acres (R's `mean of x`) and $s_d = 22{,}080$ acres over
$n = 8$ pairs, so $\mathrm{SE} = 7806.5$. R prints **`t = 1.0495, df = 7`**, a
**`p-value = 0.3288`**, and a `95 percent confidence interval` for the mean change
of **(-10,266, 26,653)** acres.

**Interpretation.** Some crops grew a lot (pistachios, almonds) and others shrank
(cotton). On average, acreage rose by about 8,200 acres per crop. But with only
eight crops and huge swings from one crop to the next, that average is swamped by
noise. Since $p = 0.329 \ge 0.05$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$: there is no
average shift we can detect. The interval includes zero, which confirms that "no
change" is still a plausible answer. Notice the payoff of the design: by pairing
on commodity, we never had to pretend a carrot field and a cotton field were
interchangeable — we only ever compared each crop to *itself*.

:::{note} Pairing vs. two independent samples — they are different designs
Do **not** analyze paired data as two independent samples; doing so throws away
the matching and usually *inflates* the standard error, hiding real effects.
Conversely, do not force a paired test onto data that are not matched. The test
you choose is dictated by the **design**, not by which gives a smaller p-value.
:::

(ch10-sec-twosample)=
## The two-sample t-test

### Intuition

Now suppose the two groups are **separate sets of subjects** with **no natural
pairing**: a treatment group and a control group, men and women, two different
fields. We cannot subtract within pairs because there are no pairs. Instead we
compare the two **group means** directly and ask whether their *difference* is
bigger than sampling noise would explain.

### Formula

With sample means $\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2$, sample standard deviations
$s_1, s_2$, and sample sizes $n_1, n_2$, the **Welch two-sample $t$ statistic**
(which does **not** assume the two groups have equal variance) is

```{math}
:label: ch10-eq-welch

t = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - \mu_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}},
```

where

- $\bar{x}_1, \bar{x}_2$ = the **two sample means**,
- $s_1, s_2$ = the **two sample standard deviations**,
- $n_1, n_2$ = the **two sample sizes**,
- $\mu_0$ = the hypothesized difference under $H_0$ (usually $0$),
- and the denominator is the **standard error of the difference**, $\mathrm{SE}$.

The hypotheses are $H_0:\ \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$ vs. $H_A:\ \mu_1 - \mu_2 \ne 0$. The
degrees of freedom for Welch's $t$ come from a longer formula that R works out
for you, so you never have to compute it by hand; it is usually not a whole
number. R's `t.test()` uses Welch by default because it is safer than assuming the
two groups have equal variance.

:::{tip} Going deeper (optional) — why we don't pool the two variances
:class: dropdown
This box is enrichment; skip it without losing anything you need for the
problems. An older "pooled" two-sample $t$-test combines $s_1$ and $s_2$ into a
single estimate of one shared variance, which buys you a clean whole-number
$df = n_1 + n_2 - 2$ — but only if the two groups truly have equal spread. When
that assumption is wrong (different spreads, especially with unequal sample
sizes), the pooled test can quietly distort the error rate. Welch's version
keeps the two variances separate, $\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}$, and pays for
that honesty with a fractional, software-computed $df$. Because we rarely *know*
the variances are equal, the safer default is to never pool — which is exactly
what R's `t.test()` does. (You will meet pooling again in @ch10-sec-twosample's
ANOVA cousin in Chapter 12, where the within-group mean square *is* a pooled
variance — there it is justified by an explicit equal-variance condition.)
:::

(ch10-sec-ex3)=
### Worked Example 3 — did the activity program raise daily steps? (randomized study)

**Intuition.** The `fitness_tracker_sim` dataset records a hypothetical
**randomized** study: 200 people were randomly assigned to a `treatment` group
(an 8-week activity-coaching program) or a `control` group, and their mean daily
**steps** were recorded. Random assignment makes the two groups independent and
comparable, so a two-sample $t$-test is exactly right.

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-ex3-setup
fit <- read.csv("data/processed/fitness_tracker_sim.csv")
# List treatment first so the reported difference reads treatment − control
# (otherwise R orders the groups alphabetically and would report control first).
fit$group <- factor(fit$group, levels = c("treatment", "control"))
tally(~group, data = fit)   # 100 treatment, 100 control
```

:::{important} Simulated data
`fitness_tracker_sim` is also synthetic (a seeded generator with a modest
built-in treatment effect). It is a teaching dataset for two-sample inference,
not a real clinical trial. See `data/codebooks/fitness_tracker_sim.md`.
:::

**Formula.** $H_0:\ \mu_{\text{treat}} - \mu_{\text{control}} = 0$ vs.
$H_A:\ \mu_{\text{treat}} - \mu_{\text{control}} \ne 0$, via @ch10-eq-welch.

**Computation.** Pass the numeric response and the grouping column:

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-ex3-twosample
t.test(steps ~ group, data = fit)
```

Dataset-derived from `fitness_tracker_sim`: R lists **`mean in group treatment` =
8112.9** steps/day and **`mean in group control` = 7170.9**, a difference of
**942.0 steps/day**, with $\mathrm{SE} = 302.2$, so

$$
t = \frac{942.0 - 0}{302.2} = 3.117, \qquad df \approx 198.0,
$$

matching R's **`t = 3.1169, df = 197.98`**, a **`p-value = 0.0021`**, and a
`95 percent confidence interval` for the difference of **(346, 1538)** steps per
day. (Because we put `treatment` first in the setup, R reports the difference as
treatment − control, so it comes out positive.)

**Interpretation.** Because $p = 0.0021 < 0.05$, we **reject** $H_0$: the program
group walked significantly more. The confidence interval (346, 1538) **excludes
zero** and is entirely positive, so we are 95% confident the program adds
somewhere between about 350 and 1,500 daily steps on average — a difference that
is both statistically detectable and, for a step count, practically meaningful.

@ch10-fig-steps-box shows the two groups side by side: the treatment box sits visibly
higher, but with plenty of overlap — which is why we needed the test to confirm
the shift is more than noise.

```r
gf_boxplot(steps ~ group, data = fit, fill = ~group, width = 0.6) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(control = okabe_ito[1], treatment = okabe_ito[2]), guide = "none")) %>%
  gf_labs(
    x = "Group (randomized assignment)",
    y = "Mean daily steps — SIMULATED",
    title = "Daily steps by group (fitness_tracker_sim)"
  )
```

(ch10-fig-steps-box)=

![Two vertical boxplots comparing mean daily steps. The control group, drawn in blue, is centered near 7,200 steps; the treatment group, drawn in orange, is centered higher near 8,100 steps. Both boxes span several thousand steps and overlap substantially, but the treatment box is shifted clearly upward.](data:image/png;base64,)

*Side-by-side boxplots of mean daily steps for the control and treatment groups in fitness_tracker_sim. The treatment median sits above the control median, with overlapping spreads — consistent with the significant but moderate difference the t-test found.*

(ch10-sec-ex4)=
### Worked Example 4 — a "no difference" result, and reading it honestly (NHANES)

**Intuition.** Not every test ends in rejection, and a non-significant result is
*information*, not failure. The `nhanes_subset` dataset is a **real** CDC teaching
sample of body measurements. Adult female height in the United States is often
quoted as about 162 cm. Does this sample's mean agree?

:::{important} NHANES is real, but it is a teaching sample
`nhanes_subset` contains **real** measurements, but the package author assembled
it for teaching and did **not** apply the official NHANES survey weights. Treat
conclusions as facts about *this 10,000-row sample*, not survey-weighted
estimates about all US adults. See `data/codebooks/nhanes_subset.md`.
:::

**Formula.** One group (adult women), one benchmark $\mu_0 = 162$ cm:
$H_0:\ \mu = 162$ vs. $H_A:\ \mu \ne 162$, via @ch10-eq-tstat.

**Computation.**

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch10-ex4-nhanes
nhanes <- read.csv("data/processed/nhanes_subset.csv")
women  <- subset(nhanes, sex == "female" & age >= 20)
t.test(~height_cm, data = women, mu = 162)
```

Dataset-derived from `nhanes_subset`: R reports `mean of x` $= 162.04$ cm over
$n = 3658$ non-missing observations (the `subset` holds 3,683 rows, but `t.test`
drops the 25 with a missing height), **`t = 0.355, df = 3657`**, a
**`p-value = 0.7225`**, and a `95 percent confidence interval` of
**(161.81, 162.28)** cm.

**Interpretation.** With $p = 0.72$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$ — the sample mean
of 162.04 cm is fully consistent with a population mean of 162 cm. Notice two
teaching points. First, the huge sample ($n = 3658$) makes the interval very
narrow (less than half a centimeter wide), so this is a *precise* "no
difference," not a vague one. Second, "fail to reject" never means "we proved
$\mu = 162$ exactly"; it means 162 is among the many plausible values the data
support.

(ch10-sec-choosing)=
## Choosing the right procedure

The hardest part of this chapter is not the arithmetic — R does that — it is
**matching the test to the design**. Use this decision flow:

1. **How many groups of measurements?**
   - *One group, compared to a fixed number* $\rightarrow$ **one-sample $t$**
     (`t.test(~y, data = D, mu = )`).
   - *Two groups* $\rightarrow$ go to step 2.
2. **Are the two groups matched one-to-one?**
   - *Yes — each value in group 1 is paired with a specific value in group 2*
     (before/after, twins, same unit at two times) $\rightarrow$ **paired $t$**
     (`t.test(~diff, data = D)` on the within-pair differences).
   - *No — the two groups are separate, independent sets of subjects* $\rightarrow$
     **two-sample $t$** (`t.test(y ~ g, data = D)`).

:::{tip} The fastest tell for paired vs. two-sample
Ask: *"If I shuffled the order of one column, would I lose information?"* If the
order matters — because row 3 in column A and row 3 in column B describe the
**same unit** — the data are **paired**. If you could reorder either column
freely without losing anything, the groups are **independent** and you want the
two-sample test.
:::

For the full menu of every test in the course — not just the three in this
chapter — see the book's [which-test decision guide](../appendix/which-test.md)
in the appendix; it routes you from "what kind of data do I have?" to the right
procedure.

:::{tip} Going deeper (optional) — a two-sample t-test is a two-group ANOVA
:class: dropdown
Enrichment, safe to skip. The two-sample $t$-test you just learned is the same
test you will meet in Chapter 12 as **one-way ANOVA** when there are exactly two
groups. With $k = 2$ groups, ANOVA's $F$-statistic is literally the square of the
(equal-variance, pooled) two-sample $t$: $F = t^2$, and the two give identical
p-values. ANOVA is the generalization to **three or more** groups, where running
many pairwise $t$-tests would inflate your false-alarm rate. So nothing in
Chapter 12 replaces what you learned here — it extends it. (One caveat: ANOVA's
$F = t^2$ identity uses the *pooled* two-sample $t$, not the Welch default; the
two match closely when the group sizes and spreads are similar.)
:::

:::{note} Durable skill — Critical thinking: the design picks the test, not the p-value
In any workplace data task — comparing two suppliers, an A/B test on a website,
a before-and-after of a process change — the analysis is only as trustworthy as
the match between the study design and the statistical procedure. Choosing
"paired" or "two-sample" *because it gives the answer you want* is a classic way
to fool yourself and your stakeholders. The professional habit is to fix the
design first (how were the data actually collected and matched?), then let that
design dictate the test, then report whatever it says. That discipline is
**critical thinking**: you reason from how the evidence was generated, not from
the conclusion you hoped for. It transfers to every evidence-based decision you
will ever defend.
:::

:::{note} Durable skill — Quantitative reasoning: an interval is worth more than a verdict
A p-value gives a yes/no verdict; a **confidence interval** gives a *range of
plausible effect sizes* in the units a decision-maker actually cares about. "The
program adds between 346 and 1,538 steps a day" is far more useful to a wellness
coordinator than "the difference was significant ($p < 0.05$)." When you lead
with the interval and its units, you turn a statistical result into a quantity a
budget or a policy can be built on. Carrying numbers with their uncertainty, and
communicating the *size* of an effect rather than just its existence, is the core
of **quantitative reasoning** on the job.
:::

(ch10-sec-tryit)=
## Try it

- **Shiny — Statistics Explorer, "One/Two-Sample Tests" module.** Load
  `fitness_tracker_sim` or `kern_crops_sim`, pick a numeric variable and a group,
  and run the $t$-test interactively. Every click shows the exact R code it ran, so
  the app and this chapter teach identical syntax. Launch the app
  from `shiny-explorer/` (`shiny::runApp("shiny-explorer")`) and open the
  **One/Two-Sample Tests** tab.
- **Jupyter lab — `labs/lab10-inference-for-means.ipynb`.** A guided, runnable
  notebook (R kernel) that walks through the one-sample and two-sample `t.test()`
  forms on these datasets, with starter-code exercises and a reflection prompt. On
  JupyterHub it loads the data by relative path; locally, open it from the `labs/`
  folder.

(ch10-sec-practice)=
## Practice problems

Problems marked **[Kern]** use a Kern-anchored dataset. Odd-numbered problems
have short answers in the book's **Answers** appendix; full worked solutions are
in the instructor key. Unless stated otherwise, use $\alpha = 0.05$ and a
two-sided alternative, and assume the $t$ conditions hold well enough to proceed.

1. **[Kern]** In your own words, explain why the almond-yield analysis in
   @ch10-sec-ex1 used a *one-sample* $t$-test rather than a two-sample test. What are
   the "one sample" and the "one number" here?

2. State the three members of the $t$-test family covered in this chapter and, in
   one sentence each, the *design* that calls for each one.

3. A one-sample $t$-test on $n = 16$ observations gives $\bar{x} = 48$, $s = 8$,
   and tests $H_0:\ \mu = 50$. Compute the standard error and the $t$ statistic by
   hand (show @ch10-eq-tstat plugged in). State the degrees of freedom.

4. Explain in plain language why the $t$-distribution is wider than the normal
   distribution, and what happens to that extra width as $n$ grows.

5. **[Kern]** Using `kern_crops_sim`, write the R call with `t.test()` that tests
   whether the mean **pistachio** yield per acre differs from 1.2 tons per acre.
   You do not need to run it — just write the correct one line of code.

6. A paired study measures blood pressure before and after a treatment on the
   same 12 patients. Why is a paired $t$-test more appropriate here than a
   two-sample $t$-test? What does pairing "remove"?

7. For the steps analysis in @ch10-sec-ex3, the 95% confidence interval for the
   difference was (346, 1538) steps. Interpret this interval in one sentence for a
   campus wellness coordinator who has never taken statistics.

8. True or false, and explain: "A non-significant result ($p = 0.72$) proves the
   two means are equal." Use @ch10-sec-ex4 to ground your answer.

9. **[Kern]** A grower claims the mean **table-grape** yield in `kern_crops_sim`
   is 7 tons per acre. The nine yearly values have $\bar{x} = 7.31$ and
   $s = 0.20$. Compute the $t$ statistic for $H_0:\ \mu = 7$ and state whether you
   would reject at $\alpha = 0.05$ (the critical value is about $t^\star = 2.31$).

10. Decide paired vs. two-sample for each design, and say why: (a) left-hand vs.
    right-hand grip strength of 30 athletes; (b) test scores of 25 students taught
    online vs. 25 *different* students taught in person; (c) a city's monthly
    rainfall this year vs. last year, month-matched.

11. **[Kern]** Using `fitness_tracker_sim`, write the `t.test()` call that compares
    **resting heart rate** (`resting_hr`) between the treatment and control groups.

12. A two-sample (Welch) $t$-test reports $df = 41.7$. Explain why the degrees of
    freedom are not a whole number, and why we use Welch's version by default.

13. Sketch (describe) what the side-by-side boxplots would look like for a
    two-sample comparison that is **not** significant. How does the overlap
    compare to @ch10-fig-steps-box?

14. A paired $t$-test on $n = 10$ pairs gives $\bar{d} = 3.0$, $s_d = 5.0$. Test
    $H_0:\ \mu_d = 0$: compute $\mathrm{SE}$, the $t$ statistic, and the $df$.

15. **[Kern]** Explain why this chapter labels its `kern_crops_sim` numbers as
    simulated and refuses to present them as facts about real Kern almond
    farming. What would change if a real USDA NASS key were registered?

16. Explain the link between the test decision and the confidence interval: if a
    95% CI for $\mu$ is $(12.4, 18.1)$, what is the result of the two-sided test of
    $H_0:\ \mu = 15$ at $\alpha = 0.05$? Of $H_0:\ \mu = 20$?

17. **[Kern]** Using `fitness_tracker_sim`, the mean **sleep** (`sleep_hours`) was
    7.11 (treatment) vs. 6.83 (control), with a two-sample $t = 1.99$,
    $df \approx 196$, $p = 0.048$. State the conclusion at $\alpha = 0.05$, and
    explain why you should be cautious calling a $p = 0.048$ result a big effect.

18. A colleague runs a two-sample $t$-test on data that are actually paired
    (before/after on the same people). Will ignoring the pairing tend to make the
    standard error too big or too small, and how could that change the conclusion?

19. **[Kern]** For the almond one-sample test in @ch10-sec-ex1 ($t = 1.41$, $df = 8$,
    $p = 0.197$), suppose a grower says "the p-value is above 0.05, so the mean
    yield is definitely exactly one ton per acre." Correct this statement.

20. List the two conditions a one-sample $t$-test requires, and for the
    nine-value almond sample, explain how @ch10-fig-almond-hist helps you check the
    normality condition.

21. A study compares mean wait times at two clinics: clinic A ($n_1 = 40$,
    $\bar{x}_1 = 22$ min, $s_1 = 6$) and clinic B ($n_2 = 35$,
    $\bar{x}_2 = 19$ min, $s_2 = 5$). Set up $H_0$ and $H_A$ and compute the
    standard error of the difference using @ch10-eq-welch's denominator.

22. Why does a *larger* sample size make a confidence interval *narrower*? Tie
    your answer to the $\sqrt{n}$ in the standard error.

23. **[Kern]** In @ch10-sec-ex2 the paired test on crop acreage gave $p = 0.329$.
    Explain how it is possible that several individual crops changed acreage a lot,
    yet the *average* change was not statistically significant.

24. Give one real-world example from your own major or job of (a) a one-sample
    $t$ question, (b) a paired $t$ question, and (c) a two-sample $t$ question.

25. A one-sided one-sample test of $H_0:\ \mu = 100$ vs. $H_A:\ \mu > 100$ gives
    $t = 1.80$ on $df = 24$. Without software, is the one-sided p-value larger or
    smaller than the two-sided p-value for the same $t$? By what factor?

(ch10-sec-summary)=
## Chapter summary

- **Inference for a mean uses the $t$-distribution**, not the normal, because we
  estimate the standard deviation $s$ from the sample. The $t$ is wider in the
  tails (set by $df = n-1$) and converges to the normal as $n$ grows.
- The **one-sample $t$-test** (`t.test(~y, data = D, mu = )`) compares one group's
  mean to a fixed value $\mu_0$ via $t = (\bar{x}-\mu_0)/(s/\sqrt{n})$.
- The **paired $t$-test** (`t.test(~diff, data = D)` on the within-pair
  differences) is a one-sample test on the **differences** of matched pairs; use it
  when the two columns are matched one-to-one.
- The **two-sample (Welch) $t$-test** (`t.test(y ~ g, data = D)`) compares the means
  of two **independent** groups via @ch10-eq-welch and does not assume equal
  variances.
- The **design dictates the test.** Decide paired vs. two-sample from how the data
  were collected, never from which p-value you prefer.
- **The decision and the confidence interval always agree**, and the interval —
  reported in real units — is usually the more useful summary for a stakeholder.

(ch10-sec-faq)=
## FAQ

**Q1. When can I use a $z$-test for a mean instead of a $t$-test?**
In practice, almost never. A $z$-test for a mean requires knowing the population
standard deviation $\sigma$, which you essentially never do. Whenever you estimate
the spread with the sample $s$ — i.e., always — use the $t$-test. With large $n$
the two give nearly identical answers anyway, because the $t$ converges to the
normal.

**Q2. My sample is small ($n < 30$). Can I still use a $t$-test?**
Yes, *if* the data look roughly symmetric with no extreme outliers (so the
normality condition is believable). The almond example ($n = 9$) is fine because
@ch10-fig-almond-hist shows a single rough mound. If a small sample is badly skewed or
has outliers, the $t$ procedure is unreliable and you would turn to a
randomization/bootstrap method (Chapters 7–8) instead.

**Q3. What is the difference between the paired test and just running two
groups?**
The paired test — `t.test(~diff, data = D)` on a column of within-pair differences
— needs the two columns to be the *same length and matched row-by-row*, and it
tests whether the mean difference is zero. The two-group form
`t.test(y ~ g, data = D)` treats the samples as independent. They answer different
questions and give different standard errors; pick based on the design
(@ch10-sec-choosing).

**Q4. Why is the Welch degrees-of-freedom not a whole number?**
Welch's method adjusts the degrees of freedom to account for the two groups
possibly having different spreads and sizes, and that adjustment usually lands on
a fractional value rather than a whole number. R reports it exactly. You never
compute it by hand — just read it from the output and trust it.

**Q5. The confidence interval includes 0. What does that mean?**
For a *difference* of means, an interval that includes 0 means "no difference" is
a plausible value — equivalent to failing to reject $H_0$ at the matching
significance level. In @ch10-sec-ex2 the acreage-change interval $(-10{,}266, 26{,}653)$
includes 0, so we could not conclude the average acreage changed.

**Q6. Does a significant result ($p < 0.05$) mean the effect is large or
important?**
No. Significance means the effect is *detectable* given the sample size, not that
it is *big*. Always read the confidence interval in real units to judge whether
the effect matters practically. A tiny, useless difference can be "significant"
with a large enough sample, and a meaningful difference can be non-significant in
a small one.

**Q7. Can I use these tests on the simulated Kern data and report the numbers as
real?**
No — and this is a rule, not a preference. The `_sim` datasets are clearly labeled
synthetic; their numbers are for *learning the method*. The moment you have real
USDA NASS data (register a free key), rerun the identical code and report those
numbers instead. The code does not change; only the data behind it does.

## Glossary

New terms introduced in this chapter are collected in the book's **Glossary**
appendix. They include: *Student's $t$-distribution*, *degrees of freedom*,
*standard error of the mean*, *one-sample $t$-test*, *paired $t$-test*,
*two-sample (Welch) $t$-test*, *mean difference*, and *critical value $t^\star$*.

## Resumen en español

:::{note} Resumen del capítulo
:class: dropdown
En este capítulo aprendiste a comparar medias (means) usando la familia de pruebas t (t-tests). La idea central es simple: cuando quieres saber si la media (the mean) de una muestra es realmente diferente de un valor de referencia o de otra media, necesitas tener en cuenta dos fuentes de variación — la variabilidad natural de los datos y la incertidumbre de usar la desviación estándar muestral (sample standard deviation) en lugar de la desviación poblacional verdadera. Para eso existe la distribución t de Student (Student's t-distribution), que es más ancha que la distribución normal y refleja esa incertidumbre adicional.

El capítulo cubre tres procedimientos. Primero, la prueba t de una muestra (one-sample t-test) te permite comparar la media de un grupo con un número específico. Por ejemplo, los rendimientos de almendra en el Condado de Kern — usando el conjunto de datos `kern_crops_sim` — se compararon con la referencia de una tonelada por acre. La estadística de prueba (test statistic) es

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}},$$

donde $\mu_0$ es el valor que se pone a prueba y $s/\sqrt{n}$ es el error estándar (standard error). Con nueve años de datos obtuvimos $t = 1.41$ y un valor p (p-value) de 0.197, lo que significa que no hubo evidencia suficiente para rechazar la hipótesis nula (null hypothesis).

Segundo, la prueba t pareada (paired t-test) se usa cuando cada observación del grupo 1 está emparejada con una observación específica del grupo 2 — como comparar el mismo cultivo en 2015 y en 2023. En ese caso simplemente se analizan las diferencias (differences) entre pares.

Tercero, la prueba t de dos muestras de Welch (two-sample Welch t-test) compara las medias de dos grupos independientes, como el grupo de tratamiento y el grupo de control (control group) en `fitness_tracker_sim`. Allí encontramos que el programa de actividad física aumentó los pasos diarios en aproximadamente 942 pasos, con un intervalo de confianza (confidence interval) del 95% de (346, 1538) pasos por día.

La regla más importante del capítulo: el diseño del estudio — no el valor p — es lo que determina qué prueba debes usar. En R, la función clave es `t.test()`: `t.test(~y, data = D, mu = )` para una muestra, `t.test(~diff, data = D)` para la prueba pareada (sobre las diferencias), y `t.test(y ~ g, data = D)` para dos muestras.
:::
